It speaks about coordination; it speaks about people -- that people should be inventive in how they organised their defence, that they should take their own decisions when they organised defence, especially in situations where they cannot get orders from their superiors, and I knew that this was the case in Konjic at this time. Sarajevo was besieged and the Mostar headquarters was not established at this time. So this is how I drew this diagram. I, of course, could not fully understand from the documentation which tasks all these structures and institutions performed at that time. I could not entirely understand who the persons were involved, who actually participated, who was a member. I knew from the documentations that many regulations which existed on paper were simply not implemented. If you allow me, I can show you another document, which supports this view, especially as for the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, for the time being I am not interested in that document. It is possible that my further questions pertaining to this chart will make you produce this document, so please answer. In your chart you mean that this co-ordinator has some aspects of superiority as to the structures depicted here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. I did not say that there was a subordinate position of any of these structures. On the contrary, I assumed that they were more or less acting together and there was no formal chain of subordination. As also indicated in this JNA secret document, because the general idea of how defence should be planned in certain instances was exactly working together and not necessarily giving orders one to the other. So I knew the situation in Konjic municipality in May 1992 more as one where several actors acted together and where they had contacts and made decisions jointly, and where everybody participated as he or she could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, according to your chart, the co-ordinator is not a function that is superior to the organs, to the bodies depicted on your chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say what exactly the functions of this co-ordinator were. I only know there was a co-ordinator. I do not know which functions he exactly performed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me for a minute. From the document I have before me of 18th May it seems that a coordinator was a link between the War Presidency and the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not that it was a link between two different warring groups. He is a co-ordinator between the War Presidency and the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not a link between the two warring forces, one HVO and one TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but the problem is that the idea was to have one unified force. This was how it should have been, but in practice it does not function like this, but they made their decisions separately. So the HVO, the Croat forces, had their separate headquarters, and the Bosnian Army had its separate headquarters. They took many, many decisions jointly and they did many -- they took many decisions jointly, but some they did not. So there was a certain need also to coordinate between the two rival military institutions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I hope counsel understands what the witness was saying. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I do understand. I will now go back to the documents that I asked in clarification of this chart. Your chart is entitled "The Defence of Konjic in May 1992"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the regulations in your file, you also submitted to us a document from the Municipal Assembly of the Konjic of 12th April 1992. Can we please see that document? This document is, in fact, a letter to the Republic of Croatia, written by the crisis staff of some municipalitites, signed by Dr Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is correct that this letter does not speak of a co-ordinator, neither does it refer to any structures in the Konjic municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is of April, as you were saying yourself, and the instance of the co-ordinator was introduced in May, as far as I can see from the documents I revised. This document was introduced to show before that there were also efforts to organise defence, that there was a crisis staff. I referred to this the other day. This is to support my view that there was a crisis staff before May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document number 50 does not refer to "crisis staff". It refers to "co-ordinator", so, please, I would like you to agree with me that the document submitted to us dated on that date is not -- cannot be used as a basis for the chart that concerns May 1992 and the role of the co-ordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The selection of documents which I made was done that way that I can show different institutions and different structures, civilian and military structures, in the Konjic municipality after the outbreak of the war. I mentioned during my explanation several times crisis staffs, and I submitted this document just to show that there was a crisis staff in April 1992. It is not part of this diagram because this reflects the situation in May and not in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I repeat: the document that you submitted, regardless of what other issue it refers to, cannot be used as the basis for the chart for May 1992 and for the role of the co-ordinator; is that so? Another document that you also submitted to us is entitled -- is dated 2nd May 1992, and the title is "Special Authorisation Granted by the War Presidency of the Konjic Municipality Pursuant to the Decision of the War Presidency on the Equipping, Obtaining and Distribution of Military Equipment", authorising Mr Zejnil Delalic to conduct various negotiations, enter into agreements, and for other matters pertaining to logistics or in other words, as the title says, for equipping, purchase and distribution of military equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then agree that this document does not pertain to military structures in the municipality of Konjic and that it does not speak to the role of the co-ordinator as presented on your chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I have the document on the screen, please? It shows us that there was a War Presidency and it shows us there were separate military structures and it shows us some decisions were taken jointly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but this has nothing to do with your chart, because this decision refers to the decision of the War Presidency and the Commander of the TO staff, so it has nothing to do with the structure depicted on your chart. It refers to other issues that happened, events that happened in Konjic but not to the chart. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, making an analysis means you gather information, different information you compile, and then you draw your conclusions. You will not find one document which explains you this diagram, but on the contrary what an analyst is supposed to do is to synthesise different kinds of information and different documents, and this is what I was trying to do. So these documents should be seen together. They form -- they give us the context, and I think this document is very interesting, because it shows us how civilian and military structures were acting together and how they were taking joint decisions. I think it is useful to have it on record and especially if you try to understand the structures in this area at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, I think that it is useful to bear many documents in mind, but this is not the document on the basis on which you can produce a chart that you submitted to us under number 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It gives us some elements of this diagram. There are other documents providing other elements. Altogether they allow me to draw up such a diagram. This is how I proceeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, I requested very precisely for you to produce the basis, the documents, that you used as the basis for determining the role of the co-ordinator and the chart that you made here, and it is obvious, since we all have the documents in front of us, that this document, dated April, and the document dated 2nd May 1992, do not refer to the matter presented in the chart. To what extent they can be used in some other context I will not talk about that now, but I think that as for the role of the co-ordinator and the relations between various bodies, that this document of 2nd May does not say anything about it. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document does not mention the function of co-ordinator. That is why I submitted a third document, which explicitly mentioned the role of a co-ordinator. This earlier document shows us that there was a War Presidency and that there was TO military structure or Bosnian Army military structure, and these two structures in situations were acting together, and that they were discussing certain issues, and that they were also taking joint decisions. I do not claim that they always acted together, but they also may have in certain instances acted together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, we were provided documents on 4th June appointing certain persons by the HVO to serve as a liaison with the prisoners, and of May 22nd 1992 the authority to compensate the goods in the distribution centre of Konjic with respect to sugar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that none of these decisions mention the co-ordinator, nor does it address the position of co-ordinator as presented in your chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but they speak of a joint staff, and I was trying to explain several times that there was a joint staff at a certain time, and this is a document giving evidence that there was a joint staff between Croat and Muslim defence forces. If you put it on the screen, we can then perfectly see headquarters of the joint armed forces and then you see the two structures, the Territorial Defence headquarters and the Croatian Defence Council. This is what I wanted to show you. It is not the only document which gives evidence for this. There are many, many others. This is just an example why I claim that there were two separated military structures, a Croat and a Muslim-dominated, but they were acting together, as we can see from this document. This is why I found it interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is document from headquarters of the joint armed forces. It is of 4th -- Konjic, 4th June 1992. The document itself is for what I was trying to explain of minor importance. What they say in this -- for me it was important to show there were common decisions and there was a joint staff, joint armed forces between the Croats and the Muslims, however indicating clearly they were separated institutions, even if they were acting together, and this was part of my diagram here. Two separate structures but linked and acting together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which is this document? I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have not seen it? It should be in the ... has it a number? It is "Headquarters of Joint Armed Forces", 4th June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The fifth document in the stack that was brought to your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The last document on the English translation? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Number 18/92, your Honours, which was the document of 4th June. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, 4th June. That is not directed to any particular person, just a general authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but -- yes. I ask again Dr Calic to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I chose this document to support the view that there were -- though there was one -- though there was a law saying there should be one unified army, in fact there were two different military structures, a Muslim-dominated one and a Croat-dominated one, the HVO and the BH army. You see on this document the signatures of the two commanders, when they are given authorisation. You see here: "Headquarters of the Joint Armed Forces". However, you also see the names of the two headquarters of the two forces, the Croats and the Muslims. I submitted this document simply to support the view that there were two military structures, a Croat-dominated and a Muslim one. They were acting together at this time. They have even had a joint staff. This supported what I was trying to show on this side, on the military side, of my diagram, two structures being interlinked, having relations, taking joint decisions as of May 1992 and a part of June, and then it broke apart, but I can explain this later. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now frankly I do not know what is the anxiety of Ms Residovic. What is your real problem? What are you complaining about in the diagram? That it does not show every function or it does not indicate who does what? These are not issues you can find on a diagram of that nature. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, I asked very precisely to be given the basis -- the documents based on which Ms Calic established the position of co-ordinator as represented in the chart. Neither of these documents speaks of that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let that remain a criticism of her documents instead of pushing it too far. That is a criticism, that it is faulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was essentially a link between the War Presidency and the defence forces. As to what extent there was cooperation between the HVO and TO is a question of fact, and she says sometimes it was and sometimes it was not. She was not sure about it herself. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, allow me to say that this chart as offered as one of the evidence materials and four documents that I have shown to Ms Calic cannot serve as a basis to explain the role of the co-ordinator, and the fifth document is of 11th July 1992, and that also does not address this chart at all. Is that correct, Ms Calic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, the headline of this diagram is not "The Role of the Co-ordinator in Konjic". The headline of this diagram is "Defence Planning in Konjic Municipality". I drew up this diagram to make a bit clearer how the structures were functioning at this time. It is also submitted as a document which explains that there was, in fact, a co-ordinator. It does not explain to us which functions he had but it explains to us that there was such a position of a co-ordinator, and this is why I also included this function in my diagram. So this should explain us defence planning. It should not explain to us exactly what the functions of this coordinating instance were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, you submitted the document 18/92 from 25th May where there are other functions of the provisional staff; in other words, is your chart -- so the chart on the defence planning on Konjic municipality in 1992 is incomplete with regard to that based on the documents that you provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To which extent it is incomplete? Can you please ... I did not get the argument.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document you submitted of 25th May talks about other institutions that also participate in decision-making. So based on that, your chart is incomplete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the document of 18th May 1992, which I put now here on the screen, under Article 2 says: "The co-ordinator" so I know there is a co-ordinator, "will be responsible for direct coordination between the defence forces of the Konjic municipality and the War Presidency", and this is, I hope, what I was drawing then in this diagram, a co-ordinator between the civilian and the military structures. This is what I wanted to show. I cannot see the deficiency, but maybe you can explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will get to the document that you have just brought to our attention, but, Ms Calic, do you agree that that document does not speak about organising the defence, as you just stated now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a function of coordination. I was trying to explain that I do not know what exactly the functions of this co-ordinator were. So I did not pretend to know what exactly the functions of the co-ordinator were. Instead I put as a headline "Defence Planning". Apparently the function of the co-ordinator somehow did also fit into this system. You see from this JNA document it becomes very clear, very clear that coordination is necessary. So why should I doubt that there was such a coordination function if I see a document, a decision on appointing a person to be a co-ordinator. This is completely in line with what I knew from before and what I also know from other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The submitted document of May 18th says that the co-ordinator will directly coordinate between the defence forces and the War Presidency; in other words, its role has been spelt out in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "coordination" but do I not know what coordination exactly means in this context. This is why I put this line showing, you know -- it is not a fixed position within any military, civilian structure, as far as I have seen. So it is a bit unclear, but what I know is the instance as such existed. I do not know what exactly the functions were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, in your report and submitted documents you also provided the decision on the establishment of the armed forces of Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decision creates either unity or subordination of the HVO units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO exists in the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your chart is subordination of the HVO with its headquarters in Grude shown on your chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not and also the direct subordination of the Bosnian Army is not shown on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you did not present the complete chart of the Konjic defence because you did not show this level of subordination; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got the impression from many documents and from many reports and also witness statements which I read that at least some of these institutions took at this time their own decisions, and we cannot assume that all the decisions taken in Konjic were taken because there was an order coming from a high institution. This is especially true for the Bosnian Army, but it may also be true for the HVO. I submitted some documents showing the signature of the local HVO Commander, and the local GO or Bosnian Army Commander. This shows us that they were making decisions in certain instances, on certain occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we could conclude that it is an incomplete chart, because it does not show other aspects of relationship between different parts of the Konjic defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shows, for instance, not how these institutions were linked to other municipalitites, which would be another very interesting aspect of all this. The intention to draw this specific diagram was to concentrate on the situation in Konjic in May 1992, which is quite an early period of this conflict. If I intended to show subordinate relationships, I would have drawn a different diagram. This was not my intention. My intention was to show defence planning I can and to show which institutions were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, the defence planning consists of all the elements thereof; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the attachments submitted with your report you also mention the law on the all people's defence of Bosnia and former Yugoslavia and a law on defence of May 14th and enacted on May 20th, and a Decision to which I pointed relating to the HVO. None of the elements from these laws are included in your chart; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Necessarily, because this law was on paper. It was not implemented on the ground. This is exactly what I am trying to explain. There are so many laws, but reality was so different from these laws. You see, in this law -- under this law there should be only one military force, only one army, but there were three armies, and in this municipality there were two armies, the HVO and the Bosnian Army. In other territories there was the Bosnian Serb Army. So this law was simply not implemented. I will give you another interesting example as you come to the question of implementation which concerns the War Presidency. You see, the same law of 20th May explains the institution of War Presidency, Article 40. It was in May. So when, in fact, did the Konjic authorities implement this law? It was not until October. I also submitted this document. You see, there is a certain time-lag, in this case five months, between May and October. So, you see, it took a certain time to implement such laws, and we cannot base all our analysis only on laws and regulations. We have to carefully assess the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, the document provided this morning and referring to the operations manual: is this a new manual or an amendment one? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it says exactly that it is made pursuant to Article 40 of the decree with the force of law of the Presidency, which was made in May, and this -- now the decision to create this Assembly -- to create the Presidency of the Assembly was made on 26th October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, on the basis of certain documents and facts have you now claimed that in May the regulations of the Republic were not implemented, and that is the decision of the territorial staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, published in the Official Gazette of 1992, which you also provided with partial translation among your documents; and also the regulation with the force of law of the armed forces -- this is Official Gazette number 2 -- and a Decision on the unification of all armed forces in the territories of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; in other words, is this the basis of the documents or on the basis of your own assessment did you claim that this was a factual work or operation of certain bodies in that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to explain that there was a certain difference between what was in the laws and how it was implemented on the ground. I think the fact that the HVO existed as a separate structure explains very well the way -- how these laws were implemented. Under the law it should not have existed at this time any longer, and I think it is a clear indication of, you know, how laws were implemented or not implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, with respect to the HVO can you claim that at any point, including May 1992, the HVO in Konjic was not under direct subordination of its headquarters in Grude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know how it functioned in this time, because in principle yes; in principle there was a subordination, but first it was according to the Bosnian law illegal, because this separate structure should not even exist, and, second, I do not know whether these orders did pass from Konjic, and whether there was -- the communication functioned. I simply do not November. So this is why I did not include it in my drawing. I simply do not know how it functions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you will agree, will you not, that the TO was a legal structure and that it was in accord with the regulations put out by the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this I cannot agree on, this because the law says there should be one unified army, and this apparently was not one unified army. This was two armies, a Croat and a Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, you are talking about 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are talking about a law adopted in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the defence law that the deadline is 90 days for adopting regulations for the coordination of the armed forces and the TO is going to discharge the functions set therein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of this. I am also aware of the fact that within 19 days instead of implementing this law, the common structure started to disintegrate completely, and the Croats left all the common structures which they -- in which they participated, so instead of implementing this law within 90 days, everything broke apart. Even the joint staff was then dissolved. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Ms Residovic. I think the Trial Chamber will rise for lunch. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The witness is still on her oath. Ms Residovic, you can continue your cross-examination. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour. Ms Calic, let me conclude with a couple of questions. On Thursday I very clearly requested that all documents be submitted to me that you used as a basis for drawing up this chart of yours. Prosecutor, Mr Ostberg, gave us a total of six documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have just seen that five out of those six documents do not directly explain the chart that you made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This chart does not contain all the elements important for understanding the defence plans in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it contains the most important elements of the defence planning in Konjic in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does not contain any of the elements of subordination, the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it does not. It was not my intention to draw chains of command. If I intended to do so, I would have submitted a different kind of diagram. It was not my intention to show chains of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in other words, the chart does not reflect all the regulations and the entire situation, but your intentions or your idea of the plans for defence in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also not correct. This document, this diagram shows different actors, the major actors involved in defence planning in May 1992 in Konjic. This is not my personal view. It is based on very many documents. I made a selection of six documents, which are representative of many others. All these documents, I believe, will be introduced during this case by other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report contains also the position of the Ministry of the Interior as one of the defence forces of Konjic, which does not -- is not included in the chart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that it is not included in the chart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, therefore, correct that your intention was not to depict all the important structures existing at that time in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. As for the police forces, the forces of the Ministry of the Interior, it was difficult to show it in a simplified way, because they were forming part as well -- they were forming part of the War Presidency as well as of the armed forces. It was just a question of not creating too much confusion of where they have to be situated, but under the law they were part of the United Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 12 of your report, paragraph 1, you said that since April 1992 a joint command was formed in Konjic. None of the six documents submitted contains the information which would lead to such a conclusion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the documents speaks about the intention to form unified forces. I saw many witness statements referring to unified structures existing in April 1992, and I believe these witnesses will come here and support their views here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, I asked you whether any of the six documents submitted here pursuant to my request to be provided with the basis for your report speaks that the joint command was formed in April 1992; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among these documents you will not find a decision to form a joint command, because I have not seen such a document, but I have seen many documents indicating to this fact, and I have also seen many witness statements, and I believe these witnesses will come here and support this view, but I cannot speak for these witnesses, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could have seen the witness statements from the prosecutor, so your conclusion is what you wrote here on page 12, and this is not the actual facts that you learned on the basis of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned it somehow on the basis of the documents. I showed you several documents indicating that there were two structures, a Croat and a Muslim-dominated military structure, and these were acting together, and this fitted also in the overall policy of the Bosnian government to unite -- to unite the forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will just repeat this question once again. The documents are the joint actions of HVO and TO were submitted with the dates of 25th May and later, so there are no documents on joint actions conducted in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not among these six, but there are other documents and other witness statements. I made a certain selection. I believed this was a selection which was representative of the kind of documents I used, but there are numerous other documents, and I repeat I believe they will all be introduced here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, Ms Calic, although I asked for all the documents, you gave me just a selection of documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your chart number 50 is not absolutely correct on the basis of the existing documents; it is an incomplete illustration and a simplified illustration of a certain structure in Konjic in May 1992, as is your document number 3 on the ethnic structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any diagram is, of course, a simplified version of reality, as is any book, any article, any report. I would like to stress again that I have seen so many documents, probably several hundreds. I am not capable of introducing them alone here, but I am sure they will be introduced during this court, and they reflect the six which I have chosen. They reflect perfectly all the other documents which I have seen. You come now back to this map, and I used the lunch break to check again the numbers. The ethnic composition of Bjelina; Bjelina has, of course, nothing to do with our Konjic. I got the photocopy and I confirmed that all the statistical service of Sarajevo confirmed that the municipality of Bjelina had -- the composition of the municipality of Bjelina was nearly 60 per cent Serb. So it was clearly a Serb majority area. I do not know how this misunderstanding could come up. I assume maybe you are referring to the town of Bjelina, which is not a Serb, but the municipality of Bjelina is nearly 60 per cent Serb according to the statistical service of Sarajevo, the statistical office of Sarajevo. I have got the figures here. I can show you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms Calic, I have concluded my questions about document number 50. As for any issues pertaining to the map, they have to do with the fact that you depicted great areas with mixed population as being majority Serbian populations, including Banja Luka, Prijedor and Bijeljina. I would not now go back to those issues. I think this concludes my cross-examination. Thank you very much, your Honours, and thank you, Ms Calic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I think that is all for you. I think this is all for the defence examinations. Have you any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I do not, your Honour. I just want to, before we release Dr Calic, introduce these exhibits to the Trial Chamber, and that is as exhibit number 6, expert report of Dr Calic; as exhibits -- in the document file exhibits number 7-69. These are the 58 numbered documents in the file given to you. Then I will finally introduce these six documents that Madam Residovic talked about now. They were in reality nine, because six were submitted yesterday and three today. Your Honours have nine documents before you in the documents you have. That concludes the documents I have to bring to the court, Dr Calic. I end by saying thank you very much to Dr Calic for her patience and willingness to answer many, many questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think there is a very small point I wanted to get clarified. There is a question about not having any document on the Joint Armed Forces. You do not remember having any document on the Joint armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is one. There is one. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Because I see here one dated 4th June 1992. It is headed "Headquarters of the Joint Armed Forces, Territorial Defence Headquarters and Croatian Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Signed "for the Headquarters of the Joint Armed Forces"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is not directed to any particular person, but it is an authorisation by the Joint Armed Forces. So I was surprised that -- I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have said in your report that in the joint command the TO Commander was to be the Commander of the Joint Staff and the HVO Commander was to be the Deputy Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is there any document supporting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There will be many documents supporting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you placed them on the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you placed them before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not here but there are such documents. They will be introduced by other witnesses. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. You have done your best. I do not think you can do more than what you have. It is very gruelling, almost one week of the witness. It is a detailed cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think the witness is discharged, except if you need her any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I do not think so, your Honour. I hope everything has been introduced duly. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. As to the exhibits the prosecution moved to introduce, as to Ms Calic, we have no objections to exhibit 6, but as to 7 through 79 I believe they are -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is very strange, very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. I did not hear -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I say it is very, very strange what you are now saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We have no objections as to the -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is very strange. We have even dismissed the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. I did not hear the forecast for objection. I apologise. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Which other witness does the Prosecution have?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr Branko Gotovac. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Swear the witness, please. MR BRANKO GOTOVAC (sworn) Examined by MS McHENRY

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please tell the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation) Good afternoon. My name is Branko Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your age now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 65.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you working at the present time, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation before you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work, what company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Igman in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of Igman, the civilian part or the military part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me explain to you. I worked in the inventory maintenance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How far did you go in school, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have secondary education. That was vocational school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1992 where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Viniste near Homolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that part of Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that -- where is your village in relation to Konjic town? About how far away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six and a half kilometres away from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnic background of most of the inhabitants of Homolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17 house holds are Serbian and four are Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time in 1992 when you were arrested, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested on 23rd May 1992 and I was taken to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain the circumstances of your arrest, including whether or not you were told anything about why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just that that was because I was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- can you explain briefly where you were when you were arrested? Was there any sort of military fighting, or can you just explain how it came to be that you were arrested, briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May 1992 I was in the garden, which was away from my house. My elder son was in the house, and he was arrested and taken to Celebici on 22nd May 1992. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 23rd May Emir Alic came. To give us shelter he said there would be an action, an operation -- at least that is what he said -- and he said we should take shelter until this whole madness passed. So I spent about half of the day in his house, and in the evening the police came, and my son was with Dervo Bajic and Spasoje Miljevic, but I was taken down there with the car and I did not see anything because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the period prior to your arrest were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I am 65 -- at that time I was 61 -- and I am retired and nobody asked me any questions and I was not interested in anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in any defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after you were arrested, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in room 22 for a while. I saw many things and I heard many things. There was a man Slobodan Babic in room 22. He could not even speak because he was beaten so badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, can I go back for a minute, please? When you were arrested, were you brought to the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that still have been on May 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening between 10 and 11pm on 23rd May, that was when I was taken to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain a prisoner in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For 101 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that when you were brought to the camp you were first put in building 22. Can you describe what building 22 was and what it was used for when you were first brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There were fire pumps and it was storage for fire-fighting equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other prisoners kept in building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived on 23rd May 1992 it was full of people, so that we were all packed like sardines. Can I elaborate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the slices of bread were being distributed the person who did it said that we were 104, but I did not count that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the other conditions in building 22? Where did you sleep? What kind of food you got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was very little food and water as well. The hygienic conditions were nothing, very bad, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you sleep, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since it was very tight, we would just lean on one another. That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in building 22 approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately I don't recall. Maybe 12-15 days. I can't recall exactly, because I was of poor hearing, poor sight, so I was just trying to survive the crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were kept in building 22 did you witness any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 21st May Spasoje Miljevic was taken out. He was beaten up. I saw Slobodan Babic. He could not see, he could not speak. That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Mr Miljevic, how long had you been in building 22 when he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came together and we left -- we were transferred together to hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long had you been in building 22 when Mr Miljevic was beaten? Was it right when you first got there or towards the end of the time you were in building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived on 23rd May 1992 and he was beaten on 24th May 1992. That was the very next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came back and they had taken him out, and he came back and he couldn't walk. Two people had to take him to relieve himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this happen on only one day, that Mr Miljevic was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That brief period of time I noticed only once, but several times in number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Staying again at the time when you were still in building 22, did you hear any mistreatment while you were there, even if you did not see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see it, because the door was closed, but we heard on 26th May the first group arrived from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I object. He is testifying from no personal knowledge. She said: "Have you heard..." The question she asked was: "Did you hear any mistreatment while you were there, even if you did not see it personally?" He said: "I could not see it because of the door." Unless he has personal knowledge about these beatings she is asking him about, then he would not be able to testify. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is what he says he heard. Is hearing not part of one's senses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This is part of one's senses. I was thinking he heard it from someone else, but if he personally heard it, that is a different story. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, would you please continue with what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 26th May 1992 the first group from Bradina was brought, the group of prisoners, and I heard people crying. I could not see them but I heard them and after that I heard them. They were forced -- they were given to greet "Meherba", "Praise the Lord", and things like that. Then they were singing something. I do not know what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in building 22 did you ever hear any screams or cries from prisoners besides on 26th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suffered the same trauma on 27th. There was a second group that arrived and they were also crying and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you brought when you were moved from building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what hangar number 6 was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a tin structure made like a half cylinder. I cannot recall the length and the width. It was like a large warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were kept in hangar number 6 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many prisoners were kept in hangar number 6 approximately, how many other people were kept there besides you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Also by the way the food was distributed about 240 people. The person who was distributing bread slices told us that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately where were you in the hangar? Were you close to the door or far away? Can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was at first a row that was circular and then there were two in the middle and I was in the middle not far away from the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions, what the conditions were like in hangar number 6, how you -- what kind of sanitary facilities, what kind of food you had, what kind of sleeping blankets and things like that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whatever people had to take off, like coats, and sometimes a blanket was torn into four pieces. The conditions were very, very bad. That was concrete down there, so there was almost nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of food did you have to eat, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes they gave us something cooked, maybe five spoonfuls, and a slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what occasions were you allowed outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only for personal need to go to urinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, while you were in hanger number 6, did you yourself suffer any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was several times, and I saw Scepo Gotovac, who was taken out and brought back in and shortly thereafter he died, and he was taken out with Simo Jovanovic several times and beaten. He came back and in 15 minutes he died. We could not see very well in the hangar, but we recognised his crying. I saw Cedo Avranovic between the rows half undressed, half dead, and nobody knew what happened to him. I saw Zeljko Cecez. He was taken out and beaten and brought back in. He asked for water and nobody gave him water. He was crying: "Brothers, help me." I don't know when but he shortly thereafter died, maybe within 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Mr Scepo Gotovac, can you please tell us in any more detail what you saw about what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic came and he said that in 1942 that he killed, slaughtered or something two Muslims and he said: "No, I never killed a chicken", and he slapped him on his face. He dropped down and he kicked him. Then he took him out and I heard his cries and screams. Then I heard him mention his mother and Zenga said: "What mother? Did you ever have a mother?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back, sir, to your own mistreatment, can you please tell us the first incident that you remember where you yourself were the victim of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it very well. First, my younger son was taken out and beaten and I crawled over to him at night and said: "Can you still survive?" He said that he would, and the older one was well, but was beaten less than the younger one. Then it was my turn soon thereafter. Landzo took me out, Esad Landzo, called Zenga. He beat me in my rib cage, stomach, teeth. So he knocked out a few of my teeth but it was not just that. There were several mistreatments following that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the first mistreatment where your teeth were knocked out and you were beaten in your rib cage by Zenga, do you remember anything else about that beating? For instance, where did it occur? Can you please tell us everything you remember about that particular beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. That was not far from the hangar and he commanded me to put my hands behind my back, behind my head and he beat me. My stomach, something snapped there and he said: "What are you grabbing your stomach for?" I told him "something snapped there". He said: "I'll operate on you right now."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said: "I'll operate on you right now", what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He beat me some more and then he said: "Let's go. Let's go back and then we'll continue."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that everything you remember about that first instance where you were beaten by Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But there's more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My next taking out, we went behind a hangar and he filled my mouth with grass so that I wouldn't cry and then he broke off a hoe and he beat me in the feet and legs and ordered me to get up. I couldn't get up. Then he kicked me some more. Then I couldn't speak any more. Then he was putting a knife into my mouth. He pulled the grass out and put a knife in and he said: "Why are you coughing here?" I didn't know what he was going to do with me. -- Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said Lepara was there with him. He was his bodyguard or something. I didn't know him. He was a younger man. I heard from our colleagues that he was Lepara and there was Makaron. Then he said to shoot him as if he is trying to escape. Then he said: "No, we'll continue another time. Bring him back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr Gotovac, you just mentioned Lepara and I believe Makaron. Were they other guards at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were others, but I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Lepara and Makaron, were they guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that they were. I heard that Makaron was. I knew that Lepara was. I did not know Makaron.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who ordered someone to shoot you and then said: "No, we'll continue another time"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo ordered -- Esad Landzo, called Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other incidents, any other times where you were mistreated, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Hazim Delic ordered us all for our hair to be cut. When we went out to have our hair cut, when it was my turn, he sent me back to be -- to be shaved clean and then he started beating me. He beat me all the way down to the door. Then he kicked me in the back continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This torture was the most painful and the worst, because then he asked me whether I preferred for both of my sons to be killed or myself, and I said: "Kill me." Then the next time I was taken out he took me out just in front of the door. There was a case there, a crate about 80 cms long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you out, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo, Zenga. He took both my sons, and Spasoje Miljevic out. Some other men came with cameras and they asked me whether Serbs killed Muslims. I said: "I don't know", and I said they didn't. Zenga threatened me with his finger, standing at the door, and then, as I described, the crate, he took out both my sons and Spasoje Miljevic, and then he put a gasmask on my older son's face and also to Spasoje Miljevic. He didn't put anything on my younger son. Then they asked me what I said to the people with the camera. I said that I had a sore throat, that I couldn't speak. Then they let me be. I said I didn't say anything. I can't remember saying anything. Then he asked me questions and hit them. Then he hit me, and then the older son, he couldn't stand the gasmask any more. He started to mumble. Then he took off his gasmask and started to beat him about the face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who started to beat your son about the face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo, Esad Landzo, nicknamed Zenga. Then he also took off the gasmask of Spasoje Miljevic. Then he took my younger son's shirt off and started to cut him with a knife. He said: "Please, Zenga, don't do it." Then he chased him back inside and I stayed there on my own and I had to spread my legs and put my hands behind my head, and when I could not do it any longer, when I saw that I couldn't move my hands, and I don't know what happened -- when his tongue went back into his throat and there was a nurse called Brane. Then I don't know who called, whether my older son or somebody. He called for help and this man Brane, he had a shoehorn and took out my tongue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, can I go back for one minute, please? I am sorry. When you had to spread your legs and put your hands behind your head, can you please explain in more detail what happened after you spread your legs and put your hands behind your head? Were you standing up or were you lying down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting down and he hit me in the scrotum so that I bled soon after that, and I saw blood coming out of my shoe legs, and Hazim Delic was close by, and when I fell unconscious on the concrete and when Brane Gligorevic pulled out my tongue I started to come to. Then Delic said: "Put him into my Fica car", and they didn't dare. So I crawled to the Fica but I couldn't open the door. He went to the other side, opened the door and told me to crawl in. I crawled in and he took me to number 22. Then he called the doctor, who was also there as a prisoner, Dr Relja from Bradina. His last name is Mrkajic. He said: "Will he die?" Relja said: "He will die."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not die, did you, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, do you know, at the time that you and your sons were being beaten, was anyone else present besides you, your sons, Mr Miljevic and Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The three of them and I as a fourth. I did not notice anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain for some period of time after Mr Delic brought you -- when you regained consciousness and Mr Delic brought you to building 22, how long did you stay in 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when it was when he brought me in. I think it was in early July, and I remained there until 30th August 1992. That is when I was released as a seriously ill person. I was allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you seriously ill because of the injuries you had received while you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other incidents where you were mistreated by Zenga or by anyone else while you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with other people, but I couldn't tell you anything about that, because the door was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion where something happened to one of your hands and, if so, can you please tell us slowly about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you about it. He went behind my back and jumped on to the crate and jumped -- I am talking about Landzo Zenga, Esad -- and he kicked me with his knees into my back. I don't know how many times. I was already deformed at that time so that my left shoulder all the way down to my elbow hurts every time the weather changes and even when it doesn't, and I also have a backache and also my ribs ache when the weather is about to change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your -- did anything happen to your hand on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe something did happen to my shoulder joint, because I have pain going all the way down to my arm when he kicked me with his knees. Maybe something happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever anything put on the palm of your hand, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time when my jaw was damaged and my teeth knocked out -- that was the first time that I was maltreated and beaten -- he put a cigarette on to my right palm and the tendons were burnt. That is what the doctor told me, and now I can't bend two of my fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put a cigarette on your hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo, nicknamed Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to take your hand away while the cigarette was being placed on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he burnt me with the cigarette, the cigarette was extinguished. He actually extinguished it by pressing it into my palm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else present when Zenga did that, any other guard or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a guard, but I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your hand show any marks from the cigarette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can show it to you. It can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put it under that light on the machine next to you, Mr Gotovac? I don't know if the usher can help him with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the defence attorneys be allowed to go and inspect the wound he is talking about? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can't bend these two fingers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if it is possible right now, but just for preservation of evidence that they have shown to the court, is it possible to have the Video Department or someone make a print of that so that we can have it for future reference. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Have you seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, we will cover that in cross-examination then. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. (Hand photographed.)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome. I have other things I could say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to what happened to you, is there also a time where you were forced to do something with a hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the hand grenade. He was holding it in his hand and he said to pull on the pin, and then he ran away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo, called Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when anything happened to your legs, where you were cut in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only in my stomach. It's protruding and every year it's more and more. I would like to have it checked by somebody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have testified that about Zenga. Did you know this person Zenga before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him, but the young men who went to school with him knew him. They even said he trained karate or something. However, very soon everybody came to know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the younger prisoners who knew Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Bendjo, Dusko Bendjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bendjo, Bendjo Dusko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Landzo throughout your time at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everything -- all the tortures that he did with me, you saw him taking other people out and bringing them back and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear his name on other occasions besides the occasion when Mr Bendjo told you his name? Did you hear his name on other occasions also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, there were some young men who knew him, but I don't recall the names of these young men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what Zenga looked like, including whether or not you found anything distinctive or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. He was medium height, only some hair on top of his head. In his face it was pale but more yellowish than whitish complexion. Sometimes he would wear a hat. It was a camouflage hat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear his voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew his voice well, because he took me out a number of times and I remember him the best when he said: "Do you want me to kill both of your sons or yourself?", and when I told him "myself", and the worst torture, when I went to 22 badly ill, he said that I would die within eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything -- excuse me. You also mentioned -- excuse me. Did you see Landzo around the camp up until the time that you left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered that. He has already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him when I was in number 22. I heard him in the compound several days. The door was kept open. He was wearing some white belt. I don't know if he was transferred to the police or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About when was it that you saw him and he was wearing a white belt? How long before you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was mid-August, maybe even before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that Landzo is the person who did all these things to you that you have described today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by it and I suffered a lot and I still suffer today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, you have also mentioned Mr Delic. Did you know Hazim Delic where you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him before but in number 22, when we got there, he had crutches, and one of his feet was bandaged. When we were in number 6 there were no crutches, no bandage. It was all normal. He did not have the bandage on his leg any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you have occasion to see Mr Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From middle of July until 30th August I saw him several times, especially on 30th August, when he told me -- he came to the door and he said: "Hurry up and get ready." I was afraid. I did not know what was going on. I took one shoe and left the other shoe. Then he said -- I said: "What shall I do?" He said: "You are going home. Get ready right away."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to observe or know anything about Mr Delic's functions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called him the Commander of the Guard and also the Deputy Commander. I don't -- I am not familiar with what he was, but anyway that is what he was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you ever see Mr Delic inside the hangar, hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oftentimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would he be doing when you saw him inside hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always strict discipline. He would pull up your feet, look down. Whoever would look up would get kicked or hit in the back, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, besides what you have already told us about, did you observe any other incidents where other persons were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not see well because it was mostly done in the evening, at night. There were no lights. You could hear screams. People were beaten up. So I could not say that I saw things. You could not see but you heard things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides what you have already told us about, did you have ever see the injuries of some other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Spasoje Miljevic. I saw some burns on his legs. Dusko Bendjo had burns on his legs. Nedeljko Draganic and Spasoje Miljevic is one of the witnesses, and I saw those burns on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Mr Draganic, what burns did you see on Mr Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to describe now. Draganic was in number 22 several days to have that treated and the rest of them were coming to be bandaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were Mr Draganic's injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His knees up, and Draganic is a witness, who he may be able to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to Mr Miljevic, what injuries did you yourself observe on Mr Miljevic? Where were the injuries, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me in person that they heated a knife and then they placed a knife on his thighs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is one of the witnesses here, so he will not say better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself, while you were in the camp, see Mr Miljevic's injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them when he came to be bandaged to number 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear anything about when prisoners were made to act like cars, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Vukasin Mrkjajic, sometimes in the evening, sometimes day time he would go around saying: "Beep, beep"; and then somebody would say: "Left blinker; right blinker." Sometimes he would have to sing. Sometimes he cried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information about who it was that made him act like a car, go: "Beep, beep" and other things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me personally that it was Hazim Delic who forced him to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any -- did you ever hear this or did you ever hear Mr Delic's voice while this was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to be frank, I could hear a voice, but I told you in advance that my hearing is poor, and I can't really tell whose the voice was, but he told me that he was the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any injuries on Mirko Babic, or did you observe his physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went from Bjelovcina to the town of Konjic on the occasion of his arrest and he was beaten and maltreated, and he was again abused and beaten in Celebici. He complained to us and that two or three of his ribs were injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. He is testifying from no personal knowledge. The question was whether he saw the injuries. That would mean he would have personal knowledge of that, but what actually happened to Mirko Babic, unless he saw it, he does not know. So he is testifying with lack of personal knowledge. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I hear him say Mirko Babic told him. Am I correct that he said he told him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what Babic told me, that he had injuries to three of his ribs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, that would still be lack of his personal knowledge. Somebody else told him that -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Somebody else? The person affected told him. The person who was beaten told him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I know there is a ruling on hearsay but that is still no personal knowledge about what happened to Mr Babic, only what somebody else told him. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not know whether Babic is someone else to him for telling him what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My objection is just that he did not see it. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is not necessary. You have raised an objection. I hear but think it is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Babic can tell him things which happened to him; he did not say he saw that thing himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am certainly not going to argue with the court at all on this issue. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can if you really want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, I do not really want to. Just in my country, and I know this is not my country, that is, of course, called hearsay. I know there are certain areas in this proceedings where hearsay is allowed. My objection is that Mr Gotovac did not see Mirko Babic being beaten, so he has no actual personal knowledge other than what someone else told him. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You had better go back to the hearsay rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is corroborative evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, in addition to what Mr Babic told you when he was at the camp, did you ever see his physical condition, for instance his ability to walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. The prosecutor is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in no condition at all. He was in a really bad way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Gotovac. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: She can ask about whether he saw injuries, but then she is telling him what the injuries are in her question. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So she is leading. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Did he see Babic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, did you ever see anything unusual about Mr Babic's physical condition when he was at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what was unusual, he was always very close to me, he was in a bad way, broken down. He was very weak, and we could not say anything to each other. We were not allowed to. We had to look straight ahead. We were not allowed to even whisper to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, going to the time that you were brought by Mr Delic back to building 22 for treatment, can you describe the building at that time -- can you describe what it was used for and what the conditions were like at that time in building 22?
